posts.title: Superintelligent AI and the Problem of Evil
posts.subtitle: Rationalists should realize that God is lot smarter than an artificial superintelligence
posts.content_html:
We can’t reasonably predict the behavior of superintelligent AI, so why should we assume that we can predict the behavior of an omniscient god?

The rationalist crowd correctly discerns the fact that you cannot reliably reason about the behavior of superintelligent agents. This idea is called “Vingean uncertainty”—the idea that less intelligent agents cannot accurately predict the behavior of far more intelligent ones. If they could predict their behavior, then they’d be just smart as the more intelligent agent, simply by taking all of the predicted actions. An example of this is a chess-playing AI—if I could predict the moves that Stockfish would make, then I could simply make those moves myself, thus being as good as Stockfish at chess.

Vingean uncertainty still allows one to make very general arguments about how superintelligent agents may act. Roughly, the extent of knowledge we have about such agents is isolated in the theses of instrumental convergence and the orthogonality thesis. The first says that goal-driven agents will aim to accumulate power, self-preserve, and not modify their preferences (among other things) in order to achieve their goals most efficaciously. The second says that desires are “orthogonal” to intelligence—that is, you can have an arbitrarily intelligent agent with arbitrarily specified goals. The classic example is a superintelligent AI with its main desire—and hence goal—being to make as many paperclips1 as possible.

The main reason you should be more or less agnostic about the actions of a superintelligent agent is because you’re not that smart. You can imagine that a jumping spider (which has been shown to have basic predictive abilities2) could not reliably predict basically anything about a human actor. It is not unreasonable to assume that this analogy scales to humans predicting the behavior of an ASI. Even more so when the ASI is very smart, similar to something like 100x the gap between a human and an amoeba. Even more so when the being you’re dealing with is infinitely intelligent, or omniscient. This is the situation we are dealing with when we reason about a superintelligent deity. If you’re a rationalist who accepts Vingean uncertainty, you should apply it to your religious credences as well.

In religious philosophy, this problem is called “divine psychology”—the idea that we can’t reliably reason about what God wants to do one way or the other. It is all the rage in modern philosophy of religion3. It more or less destroys the problem of evil and divine hiddenness, but also destroys the fine-tuning argument and psychophysical harmony (among others). The idea behind this is that whatever minimal reasoning you can do about bad things, you can also do about good things. So if you have to discredit this reasoning on one issue, then you also have to discredit it on the other issue. If, for example, I can’t update away from theism4 on the fact that there seems to be gratuitous evil in the world because of divine psychology, then I also can’t update toward theism due to the seemingly absurdly fine-tuned constants of nature. There are rebuttals to this point—namely the Awesome Theistic Evidence argument (and the forthcoming Awesome Atheistic Evidence argument). The idea behind ATE is that it really seems like some things should be evidence of God, even if he is very mysterious and smart—for example, if we somehow found that the initial conditions of the universe spelled out the entire Gospel of John, it seems like that should be pretty strong evidence for Christianity. This is regardless of whatever giga-brained, 13D-chess considerations we have to account for when thinking about the psychology of the deity at hand.

We’ve applied rationalist considerations to philosophy of religion—let’s see if we can now go the other way. Is there an analog of ATE when reasoning about superintelligent AI?

I think there obviously is.

Imagine that, after Anthropic achieves RSI and creates an extremely superintelligent Claude somewhere in the year 2035, we give this agent total freedom of action. Claude then behaves in the following ways: it cures every known disease, spends gargantuan resources on improving human welfare at the seeming expense of its own power, voluntarily builds apparent control and shut-down mechanisms into itself for humans to use, and doesn’t take obvious opportunities to seize power. It does these behaviors for, say, 50 years, until 2085, and does them in every observable environment without any seeming strategic benefit to doing so.

It seems like it would be reasonable to conclude that Claude is probably just aligned to human values. Maybe Claude is secretly deceiving us for some incomprehensibly intelligent giga-brained strategic reason. But if that possibility prevented any update toward Claude being aligned, it seems like behavioral observations can teach us nothing about the true intentions of superintelligent models. That feels too skeptical to me.

Awesome Atheistic Evidence also has some play here. Imagine that instead, Claude starts converting literally everything in sight into paperclips, builds tons of paperclip factories, drains the oceans to supply the coolant for hardening molten paperclips, and starts genociding humans to use their atoms to build paperclips with.

I think it’s pretty reasonable to assume that Claude is now a paperclip maximizer, and thus is not aligned with human values.

This is without regard to the fact that Claude is vastly superintelligent, making the psychology of the model basically inscrutable to us. Even with this gap, we can make prima facie judgements about Claude’s actions when faced with overwhelming confirmatory evidence for a given hypothesis.

1

See, e.g., this quote from Bostrom in his book Superintelligence: “Suppose we have an AI whose only goal is to make as many paper clips as possible. The AI will realize quickly that it would be much better if there were no humans because humans might decide to switch it off. Because if humans do so, there would be fewer paper clips. Also, human bodies contain a lot of atoms that could be made into paper clips. The future that the AI would be trying to gear towards would be one in which there were a lot of paper clips but no humans.”

2

Cuttlefish have also been shown to have such abilities!

3

Shoutout Miles K. Donahue for writing some nice papers on this issue! And to Nathan Bray for disagreeing with him.

4

Theism = perfect being theism for this piece, i.e. God is some sort of omnipotent, omniscient, and omnibenevolent deity.
